This is a major patch (D102/D105/D106) that changes the primary metric from K≥4 to PermG fwd + K≥3(3σ). Let me understand the scope:

1. Table 7 needs to be rewritten with new data
2. Methods section needs threshold_onset limitation paragraph
3. All references to K≥4 as primary metric need updating to PermG fwd + K≥3
4. Discussion needs GPT-2m bidirectional coupling paragraph
5. Cross-architecture statistics need updating

Let me first read the current state of the relevant files to understand what needs to change.


The core issue is that K≥4 was my primary narrative metric from earlier patches, but those numbers are now unreliable due to downstream pair inconsistencies. Meanwhile, threshold_onset has a bug that makes it essentially non-functional at true 3σ, so the MMCT approach defaults to 4-method consensus. PermG fwd is the robust metric here—it consistently shows 6-8/8 across architectures, with only Pythia-1.4B at seed 42 dropping to 2/8.

Now I need to locate Table 7 and audit all K≥4 references to see what needs updating.

\paragraph{Architecture generalization.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes across all three decoder-only transformer families tested to date.
All models reach Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) with 6/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs confirmed.
Permutation Granger forward significance is consistent across architectures (6/8 in all three), while reverse significance ranges from 2/8 to 3/8, concentrated in distinct$\to$ECE pairs consistent with the bidirectional coupling identified in \S\ref{sec:case_study}.

Method-level variation across architectures is informative.
Threshold onset detection reaches 8/8 on both GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B, where token entropy exhibits a pronounced generation-0$\to$1 discontinuity that cleanly exceeds the onset threshold.
Toda--Yamamoto ranges from 4/8 (Pythia-410M) to 6/8 (OPT-1.3B), with GPT-2-medium at 5/8, consistent with its known sensitivity to residual degrees of freedom at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
All three architectures converge at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (6/8 each).
MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) exceeds the uniform threshold on GPT-2-medium (8/8 vs.\ 6/8), demonstrating that FPR-inverse weighting recovers additional signal that the ad-hoc $K{\geq}4/5$ threshold misses.

\paragraph{Cross-condition patterns.}
Two structural patterns emerge across all generalization conditions.
First, canary$\to$perplexity pairs yield 0/14 at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus across all conditions in Table~\ref{tab:generalization}, confirming that the spurious-channel finding from \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity} is not architecture-specific but a structural property of the canary$\to$perplexity relationship: perplexity co-moves synchronously with canary metrics rather than lagging them, regardless of model family or training domain.
This elevates the perplexity channel result from a single-condition diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:case_study}) to a cross-validated finding: diversity collapse is the predictable downstream dimension, perplexity is not.
Second, restricting to canary$\to$diversity pairs (excluding the structurally non-predictable perplexity channel), 41 of 42 pairs across all conditions achieve $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (97.6\%), with the sole exception in the Pythia-1.4B seed=42 condition.
This near-perfect diversity-specific consensus validates that the framework reliably identifies the predictable dimension of iterative training collapse across architectures, scales, and domains.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Scaling from 410M to 1.4B parameters within the Pythia family yields seed-dependent consensus.
Seed 42 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}5/8$ with permutation Granger at 5/8 forward and 0/8 reverse, while seed 43 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ with 6/8 forward and 2/8 reverse (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
The weaker seed-42 result (the only condition below 6/8 consensus) reflects Toda--Yamamoto yielding 0/8, consistent with its known power limitations at short series lengths.
Permutation Granger reverse pairs that reach significance (2/8 in s43) all involve ECE in the distinct$\to$ECE direction, consistent with the bidirectional coupling pattern observed in the baseline (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Token entropy maintains 0/8 reverse across both seeds.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 confirms that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.
Pythia-1B on C4 achieves $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ in both seeds (s42, s43), with permutation Granger at 6/8 forward in both seeds.
Reverse significance is seed-dependent: s42 yields 3/8 reverse (all ECE pairs) while s43 yields 0/8 reverse, consistent with ECE's bidirectional coupling being more pronounced in certain stochastic realizations.
Token entropy maintains perfect unidirectionality (0/4 reverse) in both seeds, confirming its superiority as a directional canary across domains.

\paragraph{Architecture generalization.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes across all three decoder-only transformer families tested to date.
All models reach Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) with 6/8 canary$\to$downstream pairs confirmed.
Permutation Granger forward significance is consistent across architectures (6/8 in all three), while reverse significance ranges from 2/8 to 3/8, concentrated in distinct$\to$ECE pairs consistent with the bidirectional coupling identified in \S\ref{sec:case_study}.

Method-level variation across architectures is informative.
Threshold onset detection reaches 8/8 on both GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B, where token entropy exhibits a pronounced generation-0$\to$1 discontinuity that cleanly exceeds the onset threshold.
Toda--Yamamoto ranges from 4/8 (Pythia-410M) to 6/8 (OPT-1.3B), with GPT-2-medium at 5/8, consistent with its known sensitivity to residual degrees of freedom at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
All three architectures converge at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (6/8 each).
MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) exceeds the uniform threshold on GPT-2-medium (8/8 vs.\ 6/8), demonstrating that FPR-inverse weighting recovers additional signal that the ad-hoc $K{\geq}4/5$ threshold misses.

\paragraph{Cross-condition patterns.}
Two structural patterns emerge across all generalization conditions.
First, canary$\to$perplexity pairs yield 0/14 at $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus across all conditions in Table~\ref{tab:generalization}, confirming that the spurious-channel finding from \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity} is not architecture-specific but a structural property of the canary$\to$perplexity relationship: perplexity co-moves synchronously with canary metrics rather than lagging them, regardless of model family or training domain.
This elevates the perplexity channel result from a single-condition diagnostic (\S\ref{sec:case_study}) to a cross-validated finding: diversity collapse is the predictable downstream dimension, perplexity is not.
Second, restricting to canary$\to$diversity pairs (excluding the structurally non-predictable perplexity channel), 41 of 42 pairs across all conditions achieve $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus (97.6\%), with the sole exception in the Pythia-1.4B seed=42 condition.
This near-perfect diversity-specific consensus validates that the framework reliably identifies the predictable dimension of iterative training collapse across architectures, scales, and domains.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Scaling from 410M to 1.4B parameters within the Pythia family yields seed-dependent consensus.
Seed 42 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}5/8$ with permutation Granger at 5/8 forward and 0/8 reverse, while seed 43 produces $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ with 6/8 forward and 2/8 reverse (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
The weaker seed-42 result (the only condition below 6/8 consensus) reflects Toda--Yamamoto yielding 0/8, consistent with its known power limitations at short series lengths.
Permutation Granger reverse pairs that reach significance (2/8 in s43) all involve ECE in the distinct$\to$ECE direction, consistent with the bidirectional coupling pattern observed in the baseline (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Token entropy maintains 0/8 reverse across both seeds.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 confirms that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.
Pythia-1B on C4 achieves $K{\geq}4/5{=}6/8$ in both seeds (s42, s43), with permutation Granger at 6/8 forward in both seeds.
Reverse significance is seed-dependent: s42 yields 3/8 reverse (all ECE pairs) while s43 yields 0/8 reverse, consistent with ECE's bidirectional coupling being more pronounced in certain stochastic realizations.
Token entropy maintains perfect unidirectionality (0/4 reverse) in both seeds, confirming its superiority as a directional canary across domains.

\paragraph{Cross-condition robustness.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern is robust across 11 architecture-seed combinations spanning five model families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, Padding-variant), scales from 410M to 6.9B, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 11 conditions (90.9\%), with the sole exception being Pythia-1.4B seed~42 (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43.
$K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) mirrors permutation Granger exactly in all 11 conditions, confirming that the three-method consensus threshold provides equivalent detection power without relying on any single method.

$K{\geq}4$ ($3\sigma$) is substantially less stable (range: 0/8--6/8, median 3/8), reflecting the near-zero power of threshold onset detection under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}): threshold onset yields 0/8 in 7 of 11 conditions and at most 2/8 in the remainder, making it a de facto abstainer that inflates the $K{\geq}4$ requirement without contributing discriminative signal.
This instability motivates our use of PermG~fwd and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) as primary indicators rather than $K{\geq}4$.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Scaling from 410M to 6.9B parameters confirms that the lead-lag pattern persists across a $17\times$ parameter range.
Pythia-6.9B achieves PermG fwd~7/8 and $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$, the strongest consensus of any single-seed condition.
Within the Pythia family, 1.4B shows seed dependence: s42 yields only 2/8 (the sole outlier across all conditions), while s43 recovers to 6/8.
The Qwen3.5-0.8B result (PermG~fwd~8/8, $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$) extends the finding beyond the Pythia/GPT-2/OPT decoder-only family to an independently trained architecture with a different tokenizer.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection: Pythia-1B achieves PermG~fwd~8/8 and $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$ in both seeds, confirming that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.

133	\label{sec:mmct}

135	The uniform threshold ($K{\geq}4/5$) achieves FPR${=}$0\% and FNR${=}$0\% on reference extremes (\S\ref{sec:calibration}), but this ad-hoc threshold lacks formal statistical grounding: null-calibrated permutation testing assigns $p{=}0.16$ to $K{\geq}4/5$, failing to reach significance at conventional levels.
136	The threshold also treats all methods equally, despite the heterogeneous error profiles documented in \S\ref{sec:pitfalls}: naive cross-correlation has 100\% null-control FPR while permutation Granger has 0\%.
137	We formalize the \emph{Multi-Method Consensus Test} (MMCT), a weighted consensus framework that assigns each method influence proportional to its empirical specificity, following the specification curve tradition~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} in which analytical choices are systematically varied and aggregated rather than arbitrarily fixed~\cite{bell2022modeling}.
138	We do not claim a novel statistical method; MMCT is a consensus testing protocol adapted to the specific constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.

+\paragraph{Threshold onset detection: power limitations at $3\sigma$.}
+\label{sec:threshold_limitation}
+Post-hoc validation of the threshold onset implementation (M028) revealed that the published $2\sigma$ calibration was mislabeled as $3\sigma$.

+Under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration, threshold onset yields 0/8 significant pairs in 7 of 11 cross-architecture conditions (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}) and at most 2/8 in the remainder, reducing it to a near-zero-power method at $T{=}11$ generations.

+This low power is expected: with only 10 generation-over-generation differences, the null variance estimate has few degrees of freedom, and a $3\sigma$ exceedance threshold becomes overly conservative.

+As a consequence, the $K$-of-$M$ consensus framework effectively operates as a 4-method panel (naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, permutation Granger, Toda--Yamamoto), with threshold onset abstaining in most conditions.

+We retain threshold onset in the methodology for completeness and report its results transparently, but adopt $K{\geq}3$ (of 4 effective methods) and permutation Granger forward significance as the primary detection indicators in cross-architecture analyses.

\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds, and $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus likewise reaches 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
The transition from undetectable to reliably detectable occurs sharply between $\alpha{=}0.25$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32), the strongest individual pair (entropy$\to$distinct-1) yields a borderline signal (permutation Granger raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), while all aggregate indicators remain at null ($K{\geq}4/5{=}0/8$, MMCT${=}$0/8).
This borderline result marks the onset of the phase boundary rather than a clean null, placing the sharp phase transition at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
The non-monotonicity of permutation Granger across the transition zone (6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, 3/8 at $\alpha{=}0.60$ from a single seed, 20/24 at $\alpha{=}0.75$) further motivates the use of $K{\geq}4/5$ consensus as the primary detection metric, since it increases monotonically across all tested levels.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.

The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds ($K{\geq}4/5$ methods, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds) are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates at these thresholds.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B (single seed each, $\alpha{=}1.0$) confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: all three model families reach $K{\geq}4/5$ method agreement (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}), and MMCT weighted consensus further improves detection on GPT-2-medium (8/8 vs.\ 6/8 under the uniform threshold).
Reverse-direction tests reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 consensus ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), placing it in the same null/low-detectability regime as Pythia (0/8 Tier~3) and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across two transformer decoder-only model families of similar scale.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger finds 1/8 pairs significant, consistent with its known instability at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).

lines: \paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}

The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation) through 37.5\% (differenced) and 20.8\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger: 0/24 across all three seeds).
The consensus framework at $K{\geq}4/5$ achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
Both FPR and FNR are validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension (FPR: 3~seeds at $\alpha{=}0.0$; FNR: 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), with cross-seed FPR variance negligible (all three seeds yield 0/8 robust pairs at $K{\geq}4/5$).
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.
Table~\ref{tab:single-method-errors} complements this analysis by showing the practical consequences of relying on any single method: naive cross-correlation produces false positives at every $\alpha$ including the null control, Toda--Yamamoto misses true signals at $\alpha{=}0.75$, while the consensus at $K{\geq}3$ yields the correct verdict across all five contamination levels.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
Lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the systematic biases of its predecessors.
As machine-generated text becomes prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing and often invisible risk to production training pipelines.
By the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the underlying distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
This threat motivates the search for cheap-to-compute \emph{canary metrics}: leading indicators that signal distributional degradation before expensive downstream measures reveal the full extent of collapse.
The concept parallels early-warning signals for critical transitions in ecological systems~\cite{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating}, where proxy indicators allow intervention before a tipping point.
Several recent studies have pursued this direction: \citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} proposes spectral indicators, and DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal.

Yet the statistical methodology underlying these lead-lag claims has received little scrutiny.
Whether a candidate canary genuinely \emph{precedes} downstream degradation, or merely correlates with it under shared non-stationary trends, is a question that existing analyses leave unresolved.
Iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points per generation sequence), where detection power drops sharply and false positive rates can be high~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
In the absence of proper controls, the choice of statistical method alone can shift conclusions on the same data from universal significance to complete null.
This makes the validity of existing canary claims an open question with direct consequences for practitioners who rely on such signals to trigger training interventions.

We identify four specific deficiencies that pervade existing lead-lag analyses of iterative training collapse.
(1)~No differencing tests rule out spurious regression from shared non-stationary trends, a well-documented hazard in analyses of co-trending time series~\cite{granger1974spurious}.
(2)~Conclusions rest on a single statistical method whose assumptions about stationarity and directionality are rarely examined; no multi-method cross-validation is conducted.
(3)~No false discovery rate (FDR) correction (e.g., Benjamini--Hochberg) guards against spurious findings when testing many metric pairs simultaneously.
(4)~No regime-dependent analysis is performed, despite the possibility that the same test yields opposite conclusions at different contamination levels.
The closest predecessor is \citet{du2026geometric}, who report that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models.
Their analysis, however, covers a single metric pair, spans only 1--3 generations, and relies on visual comparisons without statistical tests.
The early-warning framework of \citet{scheffer2009early,scheffer2012anticipating} provides theoretical motivation but has not been applied to training collapse with the rigor that such short, non-stationary series require.

We address these gaps through a multiverse-style analysis~\cite{bell2022modeling,kapoor2024reforms} of canary prediction of diversity collapse, the progressive loss of lexical diversity (as measured by distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}) across training generations.
Using Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$) and up to four random seeds, we apply five statistical methods to expose three methodological pitfalls (method sensitivity, spurious regression, and regime dependence) and propose the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT), a formal FPR-inverse-weighted consensus framework inspired by specification curve analysis~\cite{simonsohn2020specification}.
An extended eight-point regime map ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) reveals a canary blind spot: at $\alpha{=}0.10$, diversity has already collapsed measurably but canary metrics remain at null levels, which places a detection lower bound at $\alpha{\geq}0.25$.
We identify token entropy as a robust one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse and demonstrate that early detection enables timely cessation of synthetic-data training, reducing peak perplexity by 58\% compared to reactive cessation at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B confirms that these findings transfer beyond the primary experimental platform.
Granger precedence in our framework establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; our canary claim is scoped to diversity metrics, not model collapse broadly.
To our knowledge, this constitutes the first multiverse-style analysis of lead-lag claims in model collapse: the same dataset, analyzed with five methods across six contamination regimes, yields conclusions that span the full spectrum from universal significance to complete null.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Systematic exposure of three methodological pitfalls and a consensus resolution} (\S\ref{sec:method}, \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}).
    Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, with five methods yielding FDR significance rates from 25\% to 100\% and inter-method agreement of $\kappa{=}0.185$.
    First-differencing eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations entirely ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$); they are artifacts of co-trending, not genuine temporal precedence.
    Regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 20/24 FDR-significant pairs at $\alpha{=}0.75$ to 0/24 at $\alpha{\leq}0.25$ under identical 3-seed, 8-pair configurations.
    To resolve these pitfalls, we propose MMCT: the standard $K{\geq}4/5$ uniform threshold yields $p{=}0.16$ under null-calibrated testing, while MMCT's pair-level FPR-inverse weighting achieves FPR${=}$0\% and 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$, a $9.5{\times}$ improvement over the uniform threshold's 8.3\%.
    Shapley-value decomposition (exact 32-coalition enumeration; Figure~\ref{fig:shapley}) identifies naive cross-correlation as the sole FPR driver (Shapley(FPR)${=}{+}0.348$) and permutation Granger as the strongest suppressor (Shapley(FPR)${=}{-}0.194$).

    \item \textbf{Regime-dependent detectability with a canary blind spot} (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
    An eight-point regime map ($\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 1.00\}$) reveals a sharp phase transition between $\alpha{=}0.25$ (borderline, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$) and $\alpha{=}0.50$ (reliably detected), with permutation Granger forward significance reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 11 cross-architecture conditions at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
    MMCT weighted consensus exhibits a complementary gradual dose-response (43.8\%$\to$58.3\%$\to$79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.25/0.50/0.75$).
    At $\alpha{=}0.10$, a canary blind spot emerges: diversity has already collapsed (distinct-1 drops 39.6\%) but canary metrics remain indistinguishable from the null condition (entropy drift $-5.3\%$ vs.\ null $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$, a gap of less than one percentage point).

    \item \textbf{Token entropy as a one-generation-ahead canary for diversity collapse} (\S\ref{sec:case_study}, \S\ref{sec:generalization}).
    At $\alpha{=}1.0$, the full consensus pipeline confirms directional asymmetry: 24/24 forward-direction canary$\to$diversity pairs are FDR-significant and 0/24 in the reverse direction (4 seeds $\times$ 6 metric pairs), confirmed by four independent methods.
    Cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B confirms the pattern.
    At $\alpha{=}0.75$, three-seed replication yields 20/24 forward and 0/24 reverse (permutation Granger), with transitional consensus (Tier~2--3).
    This claim is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$); the perplexity channel is spurious.

    \item \textbf{Canary-based early detection and cessation} (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
    As a practical demonstration, we compare predictive cessation (triggered when token entropy drops ${>}15\%$) against reactive cessation (triggered when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$).
    The entropy-based trigger fires one generation earlier, enabling cessation of synthetic-data training before irreversible damage: peak perplexity is reduced by 58\% (pooled estimate; bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%)\footnote{Bootstrap CI computed from two seed-precision pairs (s42 fp32, s43 bf16); the interval reflects observed variation rather than population-level uncertainty.} and convergence completes one generation faster (Generation~2 vs.\ Generation~3).
    At $\alpha{=}0.75$, entropy drops 31.6\% at generation~1, exceeding the 15\% threshold and confirming that the trigger generalizes beyond full synthetic replacement.
    Results are validated at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (s42 fp32; s43 bf16, subject to precision effects discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related_work} surveys related work on model collapse, early-warning signals, and lead-lag methodology.
\S\ref{sec:background} establishes the formal setup, notation, and the five detection methods used throughout.
\S\ref{sec:method} distills the three methodological pitfalls into a unified diagnostic framework, presents the multi-method consensus pipeline, and reports its empirical calibration.
\S\ref{sec:experiments} provides full experimental results: method sensitivity analysis (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), regime-dependent detectability (\S\ref{sec:regime}), canary prediction of diversity collapse (\S\ref{sec:case_study}), consensus framework validation (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}), cross-architecture generalization (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), and canary-based early intervention (\S\ref{sec:intervention}).
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and future directions, and \S\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes, followed by a dedicated Limitations section (\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model collapse in iterative training.}

The phenomenon of iterative training collapse was formalized by \citet{shumailov2024curse}, who showed that recursively replacing real data with model-generated text causes progressive tail erosion across VAEs, GMMs, and language models, and by \citet{alemohammad2024mad}, who demonstrated quality--diversity tradeoffs in self-consuming generative loops for image models.
Theoretical analyses have since sharpened these results: \citet{dohmatob2024tale} recast collapse as a change in scaling-law exponents, showing that even small fractions of synthetic data alter effective scaling behavior, while \citet{dohmatob2025strong} proved that collapse can occur even when synthetic data constitutes a vanishingly small fraction of the training set.
\citet{hataya2023will} provided early empirical evidence that large-scale generative models degrade future datasets through web-scale contamination, showing that even state-of-the-art models produce training-data artifacts detectable in downstream models, a finding that motivates our focus on contamination-level-dependent analysis.
\citet{seddik2024bad} formalized the statistical analysis of training on synthetic data, deriving excess risk bounds that quantify how synthetic fraction and model misspecification jointly govern degradation; their framework predicts regime-dependent behavior consistent with the onset boundary we observe empirically at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$.
The role of data accumulation has been a central theme.
\citet{dey2024breaking} proved that accumulating data across generations (rather than replacing it) prevents divergence of population risk in GMMs, HMMs, and language models.
\citet{kazdan2025collapse} systematically compared replace and accumulate regimes, finding that synthetic data value depends on the absolute quantity of co-present real data.
\citet{fu2025selfconsuming} provided generalization bounds for self-consuming loops, establishing that a constant fraction of real data suffices for convergence under accumulation.
On the calibration side, \citet{he2025golden} showed that optimal real-data weighting converges to the golden-ratio inverse ($1/\varphi \approx 0.618$) in Gaussian and GLM settings, and that the risk landscape is non-monotone in mixing ratio, a theoretical prediction with implications for regime-dependent canary behavior.
Beyond distributional statistics, \citet{guo2024linguistic} documented progressive decline in lexical, syntactic, and semantic diversity across iterative fine-tuning generations, providing the multi-level diversity metrics that serve as downstream targets in our lead-lag analysis.
\citet{schaeffer2025position} catalogued eight distinct and sometimes contradictory definitions of ``model collapse'' in the literature, underscoring the importance of explicit operational definitions, a concern our framework addresses by scoping canary prediction to diversity metrics specifically.

\paragraph{Canary metrics and collapse monitoring.}

Several recent works have proposed monitoring metrics that precede or accompany distributional degradation during iterative training.
\citet{du2026geometric} observe that calibration error rises before accuracy degrades in iteratively trained language models, interpreting this through a geometric-regulation lens.
\citet{du2025scales} report a similar pattern across model scales and mixing ratios, noting that ECE increases of 75\% appear at 30\% synthetic contamination before accuracy drops become visible.
Beyond calibration, SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} introduces a dual-track spectral framework based on embedding Gram matrices, where divergence between deterministic and stochastic spectral bounds serves as an early collapse diagnostic.
\citet{kalinowski2026topology} proposes a topological monitoring approach using persistent homology features to detect multi-scale structural loss in representation space.
DCES~\cite{dces2026counter} uses center-edge sampling dynamics as a collapse signal and reports improvements in ECE and entropy preservation.
\citet{gambetta2024surplexity} introduces surplexity, a surprise-based metric that simultaneously detects collapse and filters training data, demonstrating that high-surplexity selection matches human-data baselines in maintaining distributional balance.

These works collectively demonstrate growing interest in collapse monitoring, yet they share methodological limitations that weaken their lead-lag claims.
None apply differencing tests to distinguish genuine temporal precedence from spurious co-trending; none cross-validate findings across multiple statistical methods; and none apply false discovery rate correction when testing multiple metric pairs.
Our work differs from the closest predecessor, \citet{du2026geometric}, in four respects:
(i)~we compare an entire family of canary metrics rather than a single metric pair;
(ii)~we cross-validate each lead-lag relationship across five independent statistical methods, quantifying inter-method sensitivity via Cohen's $\kappa$ and intra-method sensitivity via the Toda--Yamamoto augmentation order $d_{\max}$;
(iii)~we map detectability as a function of contamination regime rather than reporting a single aggregate result; and
(iv)~we treat method-selection sensitivity itself as a primary finding, showing that it is the dominant source of variation in existing lead-lag conclusions.

\paragraph{Training dynamics monitoring.}

A broader literature tracks within-training diagnostics such as loss of plasticity~\cite{dohare2024plasticity,lyle2023plasticity}, effective representation rank, and gradient norm statistics as indicators of learning health.
These approaches monitor a single training run and detect pathologies (saturated units, rank collapse, unstable gradients) that emerge over optimization steps.
Our work differs in a key structural way: we analyze \emph{cross-generation} temporal relationships between aggregate statistics computed after each full training cycle, applying time-series causal methods to a sequence of $T{=}10$ generation-level observations rather than tracking step-level dynamics within a single run.
This distinction is methodologically consequential because the short, non-stationary series that arise from generational measurement require entirely different statistical tools (Granger causality, permutation tests, differencing diagnostics) than the long, dense traces available from step-level monitoring.

\paragraph{Early-warning signals and critical transitions.}

The theoretical foundation for canary-based prediction of system failure originates in ecology and climate science.
\citet{scheffer2009early} established that complex systems approaching tipping points exhibit generic early-warning signals (rising autocorrelation and variance due to critical slowing down), independent of system-specific mechanisms.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} extended this framework by combining empirical warning indicators with network-architecture analysis, arguing that structural and statistical signals together improve anticipatory power.
Crucially, \citet{boettiger2012limits} quantified the statistical detection limits of these signals, showing that early-warning power is often negligible in short time series, a constraint directly relevant to iterative training, where the number of generations (typically 5--20) is far smaller than typical ecological datasets.
\citet{truong2025entropy} connects entropy collapse to critical transitions, characterizing it as a first-order phase transition with universality classes that determine whether classical early-warning signals retain predictive power.
The model collapse literature has not yet imported these methodological tools: existing canary studies neither frame their claims in terms of detection power under finite samples nor test whether observed lead-lag patterns survive the short-series constraints that \citet{boettiger2012limits} identified as fundamental.

\paragraph{Lead-lag methodology.}

Granger causality~\cite{granger1969investigating} provides the standard econometric framework for testing whether one time series improves prediction of another beyond its own history.
\citet{shojaie2022granger} review classical and modern extensions, including VAR-based tests, kernel methods, and neural approaches for nonlinear dependencies \cite{marcinkevics2022neural}.
A key practical issue is non-stationarity: standard Granger tests applied to integrated (unit-root) series produce inflated rejection rates, the spurious regression problem formalized by \citet{granger1974spurious}, who demonstrated that regressions between independent random walks yield spuriously significant $t$-statistics, a hazard directly applicable to co-trending metrics in iterative training.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical} addresses this by augmenting the VAR lag order by the integration order $d_{\max}$ and testing only the original lags, yielding valid asymptotic inference regardless of cointegration structure; however, this robustness comes at the cost of reduced degrees of freedom, a trade-off that becomes severe in the short series ($T{\leq}20$) typical of iterative training studies.
Despite wide use in economics and neuroscience, these methods are largely absent from the machine learning literature on iterative training.
Existing canary studies rely on visual inspection or naive cross-correlation, which cannot distinguish genuine temporal precedence from shared non-stationary trends.
Our framework applies five complementary methods (naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation, threshold onset detection, permutation Granger causality, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger causality) and requires multi-method consensus before classifying a lead-lag relationship as robust, directly addressing the method-sensitivity problem that arises when any single test is taken in isolation.
Recent work on causal method reliability reinforces this multi-method rationale.
\citet{ruiz2026causalaudit} propose Causal-Audit, a pre-screening framework that validates causal assumptions before method selection and achieves 62\% false positive reduction; whereas their approach filters methods \emph{ex ante}, our consensus framework validates conclusions \emph{ex post} across methods already applied.
\citet{yi2026causalcompass} benchmark causal discovery robustness under eight misspecification scenarios and confirm that no single method dominates universally, directly supporting the multi-method rationale of our consensus framework.
Independently, \citet{sahoo2026calibration} show that calibration metrics are sensitive to training-distribution perturbation beyond the iterative collapse setting, suggesting that ECE-based canary signals may be confounded by non-collapse sources of calibration drift.
\citet{falahati2026curated} prove that pluralistic curation of synthetic data can prevent iterative collapse entirely, implying that canary detection is most relevant in uncontrolled data pipelines where such curation is absent.

\paragraph{Analytical robustness in ML research.}

The broader issue of researcher degrees of freedom in ML has received increasing attention.
\citet{bell2022modeling} introduced multiverse analysis to machine learning, where pipeline choices create a combinatorial space of possible results; \citet{coretta2023multidimensional} provided direct evidence through a many-analysts design in which 46 independent teams analyzed identical data and reached substantially different conclusions; and \citet{kapoor2024reforms} synthesized these concerns into REFORMS, a 32-item consensus checklist for ML-based science.
Our work applies this multiverse perspective to model collapse: five statistical methods across six contamination regimes produce conclusions that range from universal significance to complete null on the same dataset.

Table~\ref{tab:method-comparison} summarizes the methodological coverage of existing canary and monitoring analyses across the diagnostic dimensions identified in \S\ref{sec:pitfalls}.
No prior work combines all six dimensions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Methodological comparison of canary and monitoring analyses in the model collapse literature. \checkmark\ = present, $\times$ = absent, $\circ$ = partial (${\leq}2$ levels or limited replication). Diff.\ = differencing or stationarity controls for spurious regression. Multi-M.\ = cross-validation across ${\geq}2$ independent statistical methods. MTC = multiple testing correction (e.g., Bonferroni, BH-FDR). Regime = systematic variation of contamination level~$\alpha$. Seeds = ${\geq}3$ independent random seeds. Arch.\ = validation on ${\geq}2$ architecturally distinct model families.}
\label{tab:method-comparison}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lccccccl}
\toprule
Work & Diff. & Multi-M. & MTC & Regime & Seeds & Arch. & Metrics \\
\midrule
\citet{shumailov2024curse}     & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\circ$    & \checkmark & \checkmark & PPL \\
\citet{du2025scales}           & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & $\times$   & ECE, Acc, Dist-$n$ \\
\citet{gambetta2024surplexity} & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & Surplexity, Ent \\
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026spectral} & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & Spectral \\
DCES~\cite{dces2026counter}    & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & $\times$   & \checkmark & ECE, Ent, PPL \\
\midrule
\textbf{Ours}                  & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & \checkmark & Ent, ECE, PPL, Dist-$n$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

In summary, the model collapse literature has established the phenomenon and proposed monitoring metrics, while the econometric literature provides the statistical tools for temporal precedence testing.
However, no prior work bridges these two bodies of literature with the methodological rigor that short, non-stationary time series demand: systematic multi-method cross-validation, differencing diagnostics, false discovery correction, and regime-dependent calibration.
Our consensus framework fills this gap.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
4	Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
5	Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
6	Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
7	Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
8	This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.
9	
10	\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
11	All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
12	Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
13	The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
14	For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
15	Cross-architecture validation across 11 conditions spanning five model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 11 architecture-seed combinations, and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) mirrors this exactly (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
16	Reverse-direction tests reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
17	GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
18	Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
19	Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
20	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance and 0/8 at $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
21	The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
22	Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
23	The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
24	Toda--Yamamoto Granger finds 1/8 pairs significant, consistent with its known instability at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
25

33	% family and tokenizer) reach the same consensus level ($K{\geq}4/5$:

36	% pitfalls and the entropy-leads-diversity pattern are not artifacts of

39	% capacity from confounding differences in tokenizer, pre-training
40	% corpus, and architectural choices that vary across families.

43	% further establishes that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of
44	% WikiText-103's narrow topical distribution.
45	% Together, five independent validation lines (three architectures, one
46	% scale, one domain) converge on the same conclusion at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
47	% [END CONDITIONAL]
48	
49	\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to formal inference.}
50	The uniform $K{=}4/5$ threshold is instructive but statistically insufficient.
51	Its FPR and FNR properties are descriptively appealing: at $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, producing FPR${=}$37.5\%; at $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, dropping FPR to 0\%; at $K{=}5/5$, Toda--Yamamoto's low power at $T{=}10$ inflates FNR to 50\%.
52	However, null-calibrated permutation testing reveals that even this seemingly reasonable threshold yields $p{=}0.16$, failing to reach significance at $\alpha_{\text{test}}{=}0.05$.
53	The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) resolves this gap: FPR-inverse weighting provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution and achieves 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$ while maintaining FPR${=}$0\%, compared to 8.3\% for the uniform threshold at the same contamination level (a $9.5\times$ improvement).
54	
55	\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
56	With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
57	This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
58	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
59	This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
60	Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
61	However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
62	The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity (3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length), confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.
63	
64	\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
65	Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
66	In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
67	In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
68	The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
69	This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
70	We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.
71	
72	\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
73	Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
74	Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
75	This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.
76	
77	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
78	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
79	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
80	At $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested.
81	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
82	This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
83	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, $K{\geq}3$: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
84	This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
85	At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
86	This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
87	The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
88	If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.
89	
90	\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
91	In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
92	A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
93	The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
94	The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.
95	
96	\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
97	Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
98	This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
99	Our intervention experiment (\S\ref{sec:intervention}) provides preliminary evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
100	Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
101	Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
102	These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
103	The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.
104	
105	\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
106	In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
107	Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
108	The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
109	The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the limited scale of intervention validation (two seed-precision pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment requires further confirmation.
110	The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; however, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.
111	
112	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
113	The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
114	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
115	The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
116	In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
117	First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
118	Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.
119	
120	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
121	Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
122	First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
123	This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
124	Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
125	Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
126	Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
127	These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.
128	
129	\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
130	We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
131	TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
132	This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
133	The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
134	This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.
135	
136	Change-point analysis under the null condition (\$\alpha{=}0.00\$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
137	Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary\$\to\ significance (24/24) while eliminating canary\$\to\ signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).
138	
139	\paragraph{Future work.}
140	Several directions extend this work.
141	Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
142	Multi-seed replication across the three validated architecture families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT) would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}2$B parameters) remains an open direction.

150	Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
Cross-architecture validation across 11 conditions spanning five model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 11 architecture-seed combinations, and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) mirrors this exactly (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
Reverse-direction tests reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance and 0/8 at $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger finds 1/8 pairs significant, consistent with its known instability at short series lengths (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
