\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to formal inference.}
The uniform $K{=}4/5$ threshold is instructive but statistically insufficient.
Its FPR and FNR properties are descriptively appealing: at $K{=}3/5$, the two high-FPR methods (naive cross-correlation at 100\% and differenced cross-correlation at 37.5\%) can form a majority with any single additional method, producing FPR${=}$37.5\%; at $K{=}4/5$, any agreeing coalition must include at least one low-FPR method, dropping FPR to 0\%; at $K{=}5/5$, Toda--Yamamoto's low power at $T{=}10$ inflates FNR to 50\%.
However, null-calibrated permutation testing reveals that even this seemingly reasonable threshold yields $p{=}0.16$, failing to reach significance at $\alpha_{\text{test}}{=}0.05$.
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) resolves this gap: FPR-inverse weighting provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution and achieves 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$ while maintaining FPR${=}$0\%, compared to 8.3\% for the uniform threshold at the same contamination level (a $9.5\times$ improvement).

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure's elevated FNR (33.3\%, missing 2 of 6 directional pairs) is attributable to insufficient residual degrees of freedom at this series length, not to a fundamental deficiency in the method itself.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
The Toda--Yamamoto procedure produces valid test statistics at all window lengths ($T \in \{5, \ldots, 10\}$), but with unstable sensitivity (3/6 to 6/6 pairs reach significance depending on window length), confirming that its elevated FNR reflects limited residual degrees of freedom rather than absence of signal.

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method consensus: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.25$, where early warning would be most valuable, the canary signal is undetectable by any method tested.
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, $K{\geq}3$: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
Our intervention experiment (\S\ref{sec:intervention}) provides preliminary evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the limited scale of intervention validation (two seed-precision pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment requires further confirmation.
The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; however, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).

First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}

First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods and explains the Toda--Yamamoto procedure's poor power in our setting.
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).

This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.

Change-point analysis under the null condition (\$\alpha{=}0.00\$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary\$\to\ significance (24/24) while eliminating canary\$\to\ signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the three validated architecture families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT) would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}2$B parameters) remains an open direction.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These pitfalls establish that single-method, single-regime analyses (the current default) cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) addresses this fragility by replacing ad-hoc threshold voting with FPR-inverse weighted consensus and null-calibrated $p$-values.
The standard uniform threshold ($K{\geq}4/5$) achieves descriptive FPR${=}$0\% but yields $p{=}0.16$ under formal testing; MMCT pair-level weighted consensus achieves FPR${=}$0\% with 79.2\% detection at $\alpha{=}0.75$ (a $9.5\times$ improvement over the uniform threshold's 8.3\%), providing the formal inference that ad-hoc thresholds lack.

Applying the framework, token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse, Tier~3 across 4~seeds, replicated on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B) with a consistent one-generation lead; at $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry is confirmed (20/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 3~seeds) but method consensus remains transitional (Tier~2--3), mapping the detectability boundary.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
8	Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
9	Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
10	Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.
11	
12	Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
13	Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
14	We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
15	The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).
16	
17	We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
18	Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
19	Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
20	Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
21	We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
22	Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
23	Code and data will be released upon publication.
24	
25	All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
26	Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
27	Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
28	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all six contamination levels.
29

49	
50	\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
51	\label{sec:method_sensitivity}
52	
53	We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
54	If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.
55	
56	\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
57	We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
58	The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{4/16} (25.0\%).
59	Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 25\%}: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
60	The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is \textbf{75\%} across all five methods and \textbf{62.5\%} when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
61	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.
62	
63	\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
64	A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
65	For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
66	For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
67	The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
68	Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.
69	
70	\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
71	Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
72	At $d_{\max}{=}0$ (most permissive), approximately 6\% of pairs are rejected; at adaptive $d_{\max}$ determined by ADF unit-root tests, 75\%; at $d_{\max}{=}1$ (most conservative), \textbf{94\%}.
73	This single hyperparameter swings conclusions from near-universal significance to near-universal non-significance.
74	
75	\begin{figure}[t]
76	\centering
77	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
78	\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$: from $\sim$6\% rejection at $d_{\max}{=}0$ to 94\% at $d_{\max}{=}1$, demonstrating that this single hyperparameter can reverse conclusions about temporal precedence.}
79	\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
80	\end{figure}
81	
82	\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
83	Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
84	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
85	Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
86	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
87	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant, a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
88	Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\% across all three null-control seeds; Toda--Yamamoto finds 0--12.5\% (1/24 total, attributable to a degenerate $\text{df}_{\text{resid}}{=}1$ case; \S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
89	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), naive and differenced cross-correlation both find 100\% significance, permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8, consistent across 2~seeds), while threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto find 0\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), illustrating that method sensitivity persists even within the detected regime.
90	
91	\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
92	Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that the correlation-versus-causal divergence is not uniform across contamination levels.
93	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, differenced cross-correlation drops to 25\% and threshold onset to 0\%, while naive cross-correlation remains at 100\%, demonstrating that even partial detrending removes marginal associations at low contamination.
94	In the lowest-contamination regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.25$, three seeds), the false confirmation rate for the most liberal method approaches 100\%, while all Granger-type tests correctly find 0\%, a regime where single-method analysis is maximally dangerous.
95	The graded response across methods, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
96

100	\caption{Method$\times$regime consensus heatmap (Pythia-410M). Each cell shows the consensus tier ($K$-of-$M$ agreement) for a given lead-lag method (rows) and contamination level $\alpha$ (columns). A block structure emerges: correlation-based methods find significance across all $\alpha$ levels, while Granger-type methods find significance only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (fp32). The phase boundary ($\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.50$) is where method divergence is sharpest (Pitfall~3). Color scale: dark = significant (Tier~3), light = non-significant (Tier~1).}

102	\end{figure}

122	
123	\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
124	\label{sec:regime}
125	
126	Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
127	We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.
128	
129	\paragraph{Raw drift.}
130	Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
131	Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
132	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
133	Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
134	At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
135	The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.
136	
137	\begin{figure}[t]
138	\centering
139	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/regime_map.pdf}
140	\caption{Detectability regime map across contamination levels (Pythia-410M, fp32). Permutation Granger forward significance rate (solid) and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) consensus rate (dashed) as a function of $\alpha$. Both reach 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$. The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$: borderline signal at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (FDR $p{=}0.053$), reliable detection at $\alpha{=}0.50$. At $\alpha{=}0.75$, directional asymmetry is robust (20/24 forward, 0/24 reverse, 3~seeds) with transitional consensus (Tier~2--3); at $\alpha{=}1.0$, full Confirmatory consensus (24/24 forward, Tier~3, 4~seeds). Multi-seed replication: $\alpha{=}0.00$, $\alpha{=}0.25$, $\alpha{=}0.75$: 3~seeds; $\alpha{=}0.50$: 2~fp32 seeds; $\alpha{=}1.0$: 4~seeds.}
141	\label{fig:regime_map}
142	\end{figure}
143	
144	\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
145	Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
146	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/24 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$ (3~seeds), 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.10$ (1~seed, preliminary), 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32; borderline best-pair FDR $p{=}0.053$), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
147	At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
148	Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
149	Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
150	Permutation Granger forward significance and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) consensus provide complementary primary indicators (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): both reach 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and increase toward full detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
151	The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$: at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32), the best individual pair produces a borderline signal (FDR $p{=}0.053$) but all aggregate indicators remain null; by $\alpha{=}0.50$, detection is reliable.
152	This sharp phase transition is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
153	Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
154	Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach significance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
155	Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime} summarizes the regime map across both architectures.
156	At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.
157

Drift is generation~0$\to$10. GPT-2-medium $\alpha{=}0.25$: single seed (seed=42); Pythia $\alpha{=}0.25$: 3-seed mean${\pm}$std. The onset boundary ($\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$) is consistent across two transformer decoder-only model families of similar scale.}
162	\label{tab:cross_arch_regime}
163	\begin{tabular}{llcccccc}

165	$\alpha$ & Model & Entropy & ECE & Distinct-1 & Distinct-2 & Perm.\ Granger & Tier~3 \\
166	\midrule
167	0.25 & Pythia-410M  & $-4.7{\pm}0.5$ & $+81.8{\pm}15.9$ & $-40.3{\pm}0.3$ & $-56.4{\pm}0.7$ & 0/8 & 0/8 \\
168	0.25 & GPT-2-medium & $-32.8$ & $+422$ & $-23.5$ & $-31.6$ & 0/8 & 1/8 \\

175	
176	\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
177	Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds, and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) likewise reaches 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
178	The transition from undetectable to reliably detectable occurs sharply between $\alpha{=}0.25$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32), the strongest individual pair (entropy$\to$distinct-1) yields a borderline signal (permutation Granger raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), while all aggregate indicators remain at null (PermG fwd${=}$0/8, $K{\geq}3{=}0/8$).
179	This borderline result marks the onset of the phase boundary rather than a clean null, placing the sharp phase transition at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$.
180	At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
181	Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.
182	
183	
184	\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
185	\label{sec:case_study}
186	
187	Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
188	We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.
189	
190	\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
191	Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
192	Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
193	Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
194	Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
195	Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.
196	
197	\begin{figure}[t]
198	\centering
199	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/metric_trajectory.pdf}
200	\caption{Metric trajectories across 10 generations at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (Pythia-410M, 4~seeds shown as individual traces). Token entropy (top, blue) drops sharply at generation~1, while distinct-1 (bottom, red) begins declining at generations~2--3, establishing a visible one-generation canary lead. The consistent lag across all four seeds confirms that the temporal offset is robust rather than seed-specific. Shaded bands show the inter-seed range. This visual pattern corresponds to the statistical finding of 24/24 forward-direction and 0/24 reverse-direction FDR-significant pairs.}
201	\label{fig:metric_trajectory}
202	\end{figure}
203	
204	\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
205	Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 20/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
206	However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
207	Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).
208	
209	\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
210	ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
211	Across 7 validated conditions (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent unidirectional causality), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
212	This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
213	This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.
214	
215	\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
216	Not all metrics serve as canaries.
217	Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
218	Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
219	The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
220	This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
221	
222	\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
223	Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline (PermG fwd ${\geq}6/8$, $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
224	The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
225	The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).
226

234	At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
235	Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation) through 37.5\% (differenced) and 20.8\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger: 0/24 across all three seeds).
236	The consensus framework at $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all six contamination levels.

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:method_sensitivity}

We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.

\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{4/16} (25.0\%).
Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 25\%}: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is \textbf{75\%} across all five methods and \textbf{62.5\%} when excluding Toda--Yamamoto, whose low statistical power at $T{=}10$ inflates this rate (\S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.

\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.

\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
At $d_{\max}{=}0$ (most permissive), approximately 6\% of pairs are rejected; at adaptive $d_{\max}$ determined by ADF unit-root tests, 75\%; at $d_{\max}{=}1$ (most conservative), \textbf{94\%}.
This single hyperparameter swings conclusions from near-universal significance to near-universal non-significance.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$: from $\sim$6\% rejection at $d_{\max}{=}0$ to 94\% at $d_{\max}{=}1$, demonstrating that this single hyperparameter can reverse conclusions about temporal precedence.}
\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation and Toda--Yamamoto, which anchor the permissive and conservative extremes respectively) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (no synthetic data, serving as null control), naive cross-correlation finds \textbf{100\%} of pairs significant, a textbook spurious-regression outcome in trending time series.
Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\% across all three null-control seeds; Toda--Yamamoto finds 0--12.5\% (1/24 total, attributable to a degenerate $\text{df}_{\text{resid}}{=}1$ case; \S\ref{sec:consensus_validation}).
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), naive and differenced cross-correlation both find 100\% significance, permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8, consistent across 2~seeds), while threshold onset and Toda--Yamamoto find 0\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}), illustrating that method sensitivity persists even within the detected regime.

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that the correlation-versus-causal divergence is not uniform across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, differenced cross-correlation drops to 25\% and threshold onset to 0\%, while naive cross-correlation remains at 100\%, demonstrating that even partial detrending removes marginal associations at low contamination.
In the lowest-contamination regime ($\alpha{\leq}0.25$, three seeds), the false confirmation rate for the most liberal method approaches 100\%, while all Granger-type tests correctly find 0\%, a regime where single-method analysis is maximally dangerous.
The graded response across methods, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.

\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
\label{sec:regime}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.

\paragraph{Raw drift.}
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/24 pairs FDR-significant at $\alpha{=}0.00$ (3~seeds), 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.10$ (1~seed, preliminary), 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32; borderline best-pair FDR $p{=}0.053$), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
Permutation Granger forward significance and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) consensus provide complementary primary indicators (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): both reach 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and increase toward full detection at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$: at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32), the best individual pair produces a borderline signal (FDR $p{=}0.053$) but all aggregate indicators remain null; by $\alpha{=}0.50$, detection is reliable.
This sharp phase transition is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach significance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime} summarizes the regime map across both architectures.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.

\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds, and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) likewise reaches 6/8 (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
The transition from undetectable to reliably detectable occurs sharply between $\alpha{=}0.25$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (fp32), the strongest individual pair (entropy$\to$distinct-1) yields a borderline signal (permutation Granger raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), while all aggregate indicators remain at null (PermG fwd${=}$0/8, $K{\geq}3{=}0/8$).
This borderline result marks the onset of the phase boundary rather than a clean null, placing the sharp phase transition at $\alpha{\approx}0.25$--$0.30$.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.


\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing complete directional asymmetry.

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 20/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
Across 7 validated conditions (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent unidirectional causality), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline (PermG fwd ${\geq}6/8$, $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 100\% significance rate to the 37.5\% rate supported by the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method FPR ranges from \textbf{100\%} (naive cross-correlation) through 37.5\% (differenced) and 20.8\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger: 0/24 across all three seeds).
The consensus framework at $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual methods while providing robustness against miscalibration of any single method (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto alone yields FNR${=}$33.3\% (2/6), missing ECE$\to$distinct-2 and ECE$\to$distinct-3 due to Type~II errors at $T{=}10$.
Both FPR and FNR are validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension (FPR: 3~seeds at $\alpha{=}0.0$; FNR: 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), with cross-seed FPR variance negligible (all three seeds yield 0/8 robust pairs at $K{\geq}3$).
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.
Table~\ref{tab:single-method-errors} complements this analysis by showing the practical consequences of relying on any single method: naive cross-correlation produces false positives at every $\alpha$ including the null control, Toda--Yamamoto misses true signals at $\alpha{=}0.75$, while the consensus at $K{\geq}3$ yields the correct verdict across all five contamination levels.

\paragraph{Bootstrap power analysis.}
To quantify detection power beyond binary FNR, we perform bootstrap power analysis ($B{=}1{,}000$ resamples from 4-seed data at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Permutation Granger achieves power${=}1.0$ on genuine pairs (canary$\to$diversity) and power${=}0.0$ on spurious pairs (canary$\to$perplexity), providing clean separation.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves power${=}0.05$--$0.20$ on genuine pairs (depending on $d_{\max}$), confirming its poor sensitivity at $T{=}10$.
We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).

\paragraph{Cross-condition robustness.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern is robust across 11 architecture-seed combinations spanning five model families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, Padding-variant), scales from 410M to 6.9B, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 11 conditions (90.9\%), with the sole exception being Pythia-1.4B seed~42 (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43.
$K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) mirrors permutation Granger exactly in all 11 conditions, confirming that the three-method consensus threshold provides equivalent detection power without relying on any single method.

$K{\geq}4$ ($3\sigma$) is substantially less stable (range: 0/8--6/8, median 3/8), reflecting the near-zero power of threshold onset detection under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}): threshold onset yields 0/8 in 7 of 11 conditions and at most 2/8 in the remainder, making it a de facto abstainer that inflates the $K{\geq}4$ requirement without contributing discriminative signal.
This instability motivates our use of PermG~fwd and $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) as primary indicators rather than $K{\geq}4$.

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Scaling from 410M to 6.9B parameters confirms that the lead-lag pattern persists across a $17\times$ parameter range.
Pythia-6.9B achieves PermG fwd~7/8 and $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$, the strongest consensus of any single-seed condition.
Within the Pythia family, 1.4B shows seed dependence: s42 yields only 2/8 (the sole outlier across all conditions), while s43 recovers to 6/8.
The Qwen3.5-0.8B result (PermG~fwd~8/8, $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$) extends the finding beyond the Pythia/GPT-2/OPT decoder-only family to an independently trained architecture with a different tokenizer.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest detection: Pythia-1B achieves PermG~fwd~8/8 and $K{\geq}3{=}8/8$ in both seeds, confirming that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.
